history: The Heian kata (originally called Pinan) were developed in Okinawa in the late 19th to early 20th century by Itosu Ankō. Itosu sought to reform karate into a practice suitable for the general public, particularly for youth education. In 1901, Itosu introduced karate into the Okinawan school system. He modified older, more complex kata (such as Kushanku, and potentially parts of Passai and Jion) and created five simplified forms known as Pinan kata in 1907. These kata were designed as preparatory training for more advanced kata, embodying key principles of movement, technique, and defence. Channan is often cited as an influential precursor, though this connection is more speculative historical theory than verifiable fact. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to mainland Japan in the 1920s, he renamed the Pinan series Heian, retaining the same kanji (平安) but using the Japanese pronunciation. Funakoshi reversed the order of the first two kata, believing what was originally Pinan Nidan was technically easier and better suited as the introductory form.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The Heian kata (originally called Pinan) were developed in Okinawa in the late 19th to early 20th century by Itosu Ankō. In 1901, Itosu introduced karate into the Okinawan school system, modifying older, more complex kata. They were designed as preparatory training for more advanced kata. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to mainland Japan in the 1920s, he renamed them Heian. In Itosu's original system, Pinan Nidan was considered the second kata; Funakoshi reversed the order of Shodan and Nidan, believing what was originally Pinan Shodan was more suitable as the second kata.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The Heian kata (originally called Pinan) were developed in Okinawa in the late 19th to early 20th century by Itosu Ankō, who modified older more complex kata including Channan. They were designed as preparatory training for more advanced kata. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to mainland Japan in the 1920s, he renamed the series Heian.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The Heian kata (originally called Pinan) were developed by Itosu Ankō in the late 19th to early 20th century. Heian Yondan contains many movements drawn from Kankū Dai, which Itosu Ankō used as a source when creating the Heian series. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to mainland Japan in the 1920s, he renamed the series Heian.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The Heian kata (originally called Pinan) were developed by Itosu Ankō in the late 19th to early 20th century. Heian Godan contains many movements drawn from Kankū Dai. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to mainland Japan in the 1920s, he renamed the series Heian. Heian Godan is considered the most advanced of the five Heian kata.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The Tekki kata series has deep roots in Okinawan martial arts and may be among the oldest formalised kata systems. The term Naihanchi may derive from a southern Chinese dialect and may be interpreted as 'internal divided conflict'. Like the Heian kata, the Tekki forms were systematised by Itosu Ankō. According to legend, the Naihanchi/Tekki series was the only kata known by Master Motobu Chōki, who believed it alone embodied the true essence of karate. It should be noted that Motobu did not create the kata; it is said that he mastered and emphasised its effectiveness, particularly for close-quarter combat. Itosu divided the original Naihanchi into three separate kata; Tekki Shodan is thought to be the original complete form.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Tekki Nidan is one of three Tekki kata systematised by Itosu Ankō from the original Naihanchi form. It is widely believed that Tekki Nidan and Tekki Sandan were created or adapted by Itosu, as extensions of the original Naihanchi Shodan, to provide additional training material. Gichin Funakoshi brought the kata to mainland Japan in the 1920s.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Tekki Sandan is the most advanced of the three Tekki kata systematised by Itosu Ankō from the original Naihanchi form. It is widely believed that Tekki Nidan and Tekki Sandan were created or adapted by Itosu as extensions of the original Naihanchi Shodan. Gichin Funakoshi brought the kata to mainland Japan in the 1920s.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

translation: Greater Bassai — To Penetrate a Fortress
history: Originally called Passai, this kata has roots in Okinawan Shuri-te with likely influence from Chinese martial arts brought to Okinawa during the Ming and Qing dynasties. The base of the kata is thought to derive from a 14th century tao (Chinese kata). The stomping, open hand strikes, and sudden direction changes support the hypothesis of White Crane and other Southern Chinese influence. The kata was passed down through masters including Kokan Oyadomari, Sōkon Matsumura, and Itosu Ankō, who refined and divided it into Passai Dai and Passai Sho versions. Bassai Dai is considered one of the most important intermediate-to-advanced kata in Shōtōkan, often required for 1st dan examination. A regional version called Oyadomari no Passai (Tomari no Passai) is still taught in some schools. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to Japan in the 1920s, he retained the Bassai kata, renaming them using standard Japanese kanji.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Passai] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

translation: Lesser Bassai — To Penetrate a Fortress
history: Bassai Sho was developed or restructured by Itosu Ankō to provide a complementary and slightly more advanced variation of Bassai Dai. It shares the same Passai origins as Bassai Dai, with roots in Okinawan Shuri-te and likely Chinese martial arts influence. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to Japan in the 1920s, he retained and renamed the kata using standard Japanese kanji.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Passai] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: In older Okinawan traditions the kata was known as Kushanku or Kūsankū, reportedly named after a Chinese martial arts diplomat who taught local Okinawan practitioners a form of Chuan Fa. Alternative theories suggest Kūsankū taught the kata to Chatan Yara and Tōde Sakugawa. Funakoshi renamed it Kankū during his effort to standardise karate terminology in Japan. It is widely accepted by historians that Itosu Ankō created the Sho versions to complement the existing Dai (Matsumura lineage) forms. Funakoshi chose Kankū Dai as a central model kata for Shōtōkan, and many of its movements appear in the Heian kata, particularly Heian Yondan and Godan, because Itosu Ankō used Kankū Dai as one of the foundational sources when creating the Heian forms.
lineage: Kūsankū (Chinese Diplomat) → Kanga Sakugawa → Itosu Ankō → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Kankū Sho shares the same Kūsankū origins as Kankū Dai. It is widely accepted by historians that Itosu Ankō created the Sho version to complement the existing Dai (Matsumura lineage) form. Funakoshi renamed and standardised the kata when bringing karate to mainland Japan.
lineage: Kūsankū (Chinese Diplomat) → Kanga Sakugawa → Itosu Ankō → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The kata now known as Empi is based on an older Okinawan form called Wanshū, whose name is thought to originate from a Chinese envoy or military attaché named Wang Ji (汪楫), also known as Sappushi Wanshū, who reportedly visited Okinawa in the late 1600s and may have introduced forms of Southern Chinese boxing. Wanshū's teachings were absorbed and transmitted by early Okinawan masters in the lineage of Kokan Oyadomari and Chōtoku Kyan, who passed it down as part of the Tomari-te curriculum. It was later introduced into Shuri-te and Shitō-ryū. A version is still known by the original name Wanshū in Isshin-ryū and Wadō-ryū. When Gichin Funakoshi brought karate to mainland Japan, he renamed the form Empi, aligning with his broader effort to adapt Okinawan karate terminology to Japanese linguistic and aesthetic sensibilities.
lineage: Wang Ji (Shaolin/Fujian White Crane [disputed]) → Tomari-te masters, e.g. Chōtoku Kyan → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Jion is one of the three Temple Kata (along with Jitte and Jiin) in Shōtōkan. They are widely considered part of the Shōrei-ryū lineage, emphasising grounded stances and internal energy. The precise origins are somewhat obscured by time, but most research points to the Tomari-te tradition. The kata may have been influenced by martial teachings from Chinese monks or diplomats, and there are speculative ties to a Zen Buddhist temple, possibly Jion-ji Temple in Kyoto, though this connection is largely symbolic and unverified. Itosu Ankō is believed to have preserved or adapted these forms. Jion was said to have been renamed 'Shokyo' by Funakoshi, but this name never stuck within Shōtōkan.
lineage: Tomari-te School → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Jitte is one of the three Temple Kata in Shōtōkan, grouped with Jion and Jiin. They are widely considered part of the Shōrei-ryū lineage. The name may also reference the jitte weapon used by Edo-period police. Precise origins point to the Tomari-te tradition, preserved by Itosu Ankō. All three Temple Kata share similar salutation opening movements and a tone of stillness, strength, and mental clarity.
lineage: Tomari-te School → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Jiin is one of the three Temple Kata in Shōtōkan, grouped with Jion and Jitte. They are widely considered part of the Shōrei-ryū lineage emphasising grounded stances and powerful techniques. Precise origins point to the Tomari-te tradition and are believed to have been preserved by Itosu Ankō. All three Temple Kata share similar salutation opening movements, related embusen and stances, and a tone of stillness and mental clarity.
lineage: Tomari-te School → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: The kata now known as Gankaku was originally called Chintō (鎮東), or Mukandi in Okinawa. According to traditional accounts, Chintō was the name of a Chinese sailor or martial artist who became shipwrecked on Okinawa during the 19th century, although some sources state he was called Annan. He was reputed to possess unique fighting skills, and after reportedly causing trouble by stealing food, he was challenged by Sōkon Matsumura. Rather than defeat Chintō, Matsumura was impressed by his skills and reportedly learned from him, integrating Chinese methods — particularly White Crane and Northern Shaolin influence — with Okinawan principles. However, putting this unverified account aside, Matsumura may simply have adapted Chinese techniques directly. Itosu Ankō helped preserve the form, and Funakoshi later brought it to Japan, renaming it Gankaku to reflect the kata's symbolism and to avoid Chinese-sounding names, aligning with nationalistic sentiment in early 20th-century Japan.
lineage: Chintō (or Annan) → Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Gankaku Sho is a rarely practised secondary form related to Gankaku in some Shōtōkan lineages. It is believed to be a modern creation or adaptation, possibly by Kanazawa Hirokazu, influenced by or paired with the pattern of Bassai Sho, Kankū Sho, and others in the 'Sho' series. Its presence is not universal in Shōtōkan and may be more commonly found in Shitō-ryū or other blended styles. It shares the same Chintō origins as Gankaku.
lineage: Chintō → Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Hangetsu is believed to have originated as Seishan, a kata practised in multiple Okinawan and Chinese-influenced karate styles. The kata has roots in Southern Chinese martial arts such as White Crane and Fujian Tiger, where controlled breathing, rooted stances, and dynamic tension are emphasised. There is strong evidence of Quanfa forms with similar techniques, linking the kata to a much older history. Many karate historians state the Shōtōkan version originated with Higaonna Kanryō, though Funakoshi's version was more likely influenced through multiple channels, and the kata has multiple independent lineages across Shuri-te and Naha-te traditions. Gichin Funakoshi renamed it Hangetsu and adjusted its embusen, pacing, and stance dynamics to better suit Shōtōkan's linear structure and deep stances. Hangetsu integrates deep Sanchin-like breathing, slow muscle control, and subtle body mechanics, and is one of the few Shōtōkan kata to do so.
lineage: Naha-te (Seisan) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Sōchin is believed to have originated in the Aragaki-ryū tradition with strong Chinese Southern influence, preserved by Aragaki Seishō who was well-versed in White Crane and Tiger systems. Both Gichin Funakoshi and Kenwa Mabuni were students of Aragaki. From Aragaki's teachings, a kata resembling Sōchin called koshiki was absorbed into early Shitō-ryū and Shōrin-ryū systems. Funakoshi briefly renamed it 'Hakkō' but this name did not stick. Though not part of Funakoshi's original 15 kata, it was later introduced into Shōtōkan, likely through Yoshitaka (Gigo) Funakoshi or other senior JKA instructors. The Shōtōkan version is highly modified and differs significantly from the Shitō-ryū version, emphasising the rooted Fudo-dachi stance.
lineage: Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū) → Funakoshi Yoshitaka (Shōtōkan)

history: Nijushiho has roots in both the Naha-te and Shuri-te lineages as well as the Aragaki school tradition. The original version, Niseishi, is widely practised in Shitō-ryū, Shōrin-ryū, and Gōjū-ryū. The kata likely descended from Southern Chinese martial arts, particularly White Crane or Tiger systems. The version that became Nijushiho in Shōtōkan likely came through the influence of Kenwa Mabuni or through Itosu Ankō. The name was standardised by Gichin Funakoshi as part of his effort to Japanise Okinawan and Chinese-sounding names.
lineage: Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū) → Funakoshi Yoshitaka (Shōtōkan)

history: The core material derives from the three versions of Rōhai taught by Itosu Ankō. The name Meikyo was selected by Gichin Funakoshi when adapting the older Okinawan kata known as Rōhai, a form that existed in multiple versions across various Okinawan lineages. The change aligned with Funakoshi's philosophy of karate as a path to self-purification and mental refinement. The kata is sometimes referred to as Matsumura no Rōhai, alluding to its lineage, though Rōhai had multiple versions across Okinawan lineages and some Tomari-te masters like Kokan Oyadomari are also associated with it. Meikyo retains little of the distinctive movements of the original Rōhai versions, most notably the absence of one-legged stances (tsuri-ashi dachi).
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) [possibly] / Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [likely] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Chinte is believed to originate in Tomari-te and to be from the same family of kata as Chintō (Gankaku). The kata is believed to have been imported to Okinawa by Chinese traders or emissaries and preserved by early Okinawan masters, likely drawing influence from Southern Chinese martial arts including White Crane, Tiger, and potentially Baguazhang or Liu He Ba Fa. Although Chinte was not among the original 15 kata Gichin Funakoshi emphasised in early Shōtōkan, it was later adopted and formalised by the JKA in the mid-20th century. Funakoshi proposed changing the name to Shoin, but this name was never used. Chinte departs from the linear, powerful rhythm of most Shōtōkan kata, featuring distinctively circular, open-handed, and unusual techniques.
lineage: Shuri-te lineage → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Unsu is believed to have originated in the Tomari-te lineage, heavily influenced by Southern Chinese martial arts. It is considered a synthesis kata drawing on older forms including Niseishi (Nijushiho), Chinte, Sōchin, and Bassai Sho, suggesting it was designed as a culminating form. In 1922, the kata was noted in Funakoshi's book Ryūkyū Kenpō Karate. It was taught from Aragaki to Kenwa Mabuni, whose interactions with Funakoshi may have facilitated its entry into Shōtōkan. Unsu was introduced into Shōtōkan by the JKA during the early to mid-20th century, and was especially championed by Masatoshi Nakayama, who emphasised athleticism and technical clarity.
lineage: Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū) → Funakoshi Yoshitaka (Shōtōkan)

history: Wankan is an old kata with roots in the Tomari-te tradition of Okinawan karate, likely arrived in Okinawa via Chinese martial arts influence from Fujian or other southern provinces. In Okinawa it was preserved through various schools but was not widely practised or systematised across all styles. Funakoshi tried to rename it Shofu or Hito, but these names did not stick. In Shōtōkan, Wankan is believed to have been adopted later in the development of the style, possibly through the efforts of the JKA to codify a comprehensive kata syllabus, influenced or preserved by instructors such as Masatoshi Nakayama.
lineage: Tomari-te masters → Shōtōkan

history: The Gojūshiho kata likely originated from Chinese martial arts, particularly those from the Fujian and Northern Shaolin regions, introduced to Okinawa through the Tomari-te or Shuri-te traditions. The original form was known as Useishi (or Ouseishi), a Chinese-style pronunciation of the same characters for '54', and is credited to Sōkon Matsumura. Funakoshi briefly renamed it Hotaku (phoenix peck), but this name did not endure. When the JKA systematised Shōtōkan, the forms were renamed Gojūshiho Dai and Gojūshiho Sho. The Dai and Sho designations distinguish the two related forms rather than necessarily reflecting difficulty or length. Some Shōtōkan organisations switch the Dai and Sho labels, causing confusion — the myth that this arose from a master using the wrong name in a demonstration still persists.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) / Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Gojūshiho Sho shares the same Useishi origins as Gojūshiho Dai, credited originally to Sōkon Matsumura. Funakoshi briefly renamed the forms Hotaku (phoenix peck), but this name did not endure. The Dai and Sho designations distinguish the two related forms rather than necessarily reflecting difficulty or length. Some Shōtōkan organisations switch the Dai and Sho labels, causing confusion across associations — the myth that this arose from a master using the wrong name in a demonstration still persists.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) / Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Taikyoku translates to 'Grand Ultimate' or 'Supreme Ultimate', borrowing the concept from Chinese philosophy and Taoist thought where it represents the source of all existence and the balance of yin and yang. Three forms formally exist: Shodan, Nidan, and Sandan, though other forms have been developed by separate associations. The kata were likely originally created by Gichin Funakoshi in the 1930s as introductory forms to teach fundamental techniques, stances, and movement patterns to beginners. His son Gigo (Yoshitaka) Funakoshi also played a significant role in their development and is viewed by many as the real creator of the forms used today. The kata were later adopted and modified by Masutatsu Ōyama for Kyokushin karate.
lineage: Gichin Funakoshi / Funakoshi Yoshitaka (Shōtōkan)

history: Ten no Kata is a modern training exercise rather than a traditional Okinawan kata with deep historical roots. It is a series of forms designed for absolute beginners, even simpler than the Heian series, providing a foundation in basic stances, blocks, and punches. It was likely developed in the 1940s by Funakoshi Gigo (Yoshitaka), the son of Gichin Funakoshi, with his father's support. It is arguable whether this is a kata at all, but it is included in the Shōtōkan kata list for completeness.
lineage: Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan)

history: Gekisai Dai Ichi and Gekisai Dai Ni were created by Chōjun Miyagi in 1940 to introduce karate to Okinawan schools and the general public. They were designed to teach fundamental Gōjū-ryū techniques in an accessible format. These kata are the entry point for Gōjū-ryū practitioners, covering basic blocks, strikes, and stances.
lineage: Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Gekisai Dai Ni was created alongside Gekisai Dai Ichi by Chōjun Miyagi in 1940 to introduce karate to Okinawan schools and the general public. It builds on Gekisai Dai Ichi with the addition of open-hand techniques and more advanced movements, while retaining the accessible structure.
lineage: Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

translation: Smash and Tear / Break and Destroy
history: Saifa is one of the classical Gōjū-ryū kata with roots in Chinese martial arts, particularly White Crane and Tiger styles from Fujian Province, transmitted to Okinawa through Higaonna Kanryō during his studies in China in the 1870s. It is characterised by powerful breaking and tearing techniques. Saifa is typically the first classical kata taught after the Gekisai forms. Also known as Saiha.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

translation: Pull-Back Battle / Conquer and Subdue Over Distance
history: Seienchin is one of the classical Gōjū-ryū kata with roots in Chinese martial arts, transmitted through Higaonna Kanryō. It emphasises pull-and-push grappling techniques and close-range combat, reflecting the Naha-te tradition of combining hard and soft methods. Also written as Seiunchin.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

translation: Four Direction Battle / Suppress in Four Directions
history: Shisōchin is one of the classical Gōjū-ryū kata with roots in Chinese martial arts, particularly White Crane and Tiger styles from Fujian Province, transmitted to Okinawa through Higaonna Kanryō during his studies in China in the 1870s. It features techniques directed to four directions, reflecting multi-directional defence and combat strategy. Its techniques emphasise fighting against multiple opponents.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi, Kyoda Juhatsu

history: Sanseiru is one of the classical Gōjū-ryū kata with roots in Chinese martial arts, transmitted through Higaonna Kanryō. The number 36 represents half of 72, a number of symbolic significance in Chinese martial arts philosophy. The kata covers a wide range of combat techniques.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū), Kanbun Uechi (Uechi-ryū)

translation: Holding Ground Form / Stay and Destroy
history: Kururunfa is one of the classical Gōjū-ryū kata with roots in Chinese martial arts, particularly White Crane, Praying Mantis, and Tiger styles from Fujian Province, transmitted to Okinawa through Higaonna Kanryō during his studies in China in the 1870s. It emphasises fighting techniques used when maintaining a defensive position while countering aggressively. The kata includes complex hand techniques and changes of direction.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō → Chōjun Miyagi, Kyoda Juhatsu; Chōjun Miyagi → Masutatsu (via Goen Yamaguchi)

history: Fukyūgata was explicitly created for the purpose of spreading and popularising karate practice, developed by the Okinawan Karate Federation around 1940–1941. Fukyūgata Ichi was created by Nagamine Shōshin of Matsubayashi-ryū, while Fukyūgata Ni was developed by Chōjun Miyagi of Gōjū-ryū. Both forms were designed as standardised introductory kata suitable for physical education in Okinawan schools.
lineage: Nagamine Shoshin (Matsubayashi-ryu) and Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Seisan is thought to be one of the oldest kata in Okinawan karate, likely dating to the 17th or 18th century, and exists in various forms across multiple styles. In Gōjū-ryū it was transmitted through Higaonna Kanryō from Chinese martial arts sources. Related versions appear in Shōtōkan (as Hangetsu), Uechi-ryū, Isshin-ryū, and Shitō-ryū, though stylistically very different.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Okinawan karate → various masters depending on the version and school, including Higaonna Kanryō and Kenwa Mabuni → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Suparinpei translates to 108, a number of Buddhist significance representing the 108 earthly temptations that must be overcome to achieve enlightenment. Higaonna Kanryō learned this kata during his studies in China in the 1870s, and it was preserved and refined by Chōjun Miyagi. It is the longest and most advanced kata in Gōjū-ryū. It also goes by the names Pechurin (from Okinawan) and Hyakuhachi, which is the literal reading of 108. It is also practised in Shitō-ryū.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū), Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Sanchin likely originated in Fujian Province, China, during the 18th century as part of Southern Chinese martial arts traditions. The lineage flows primarily through Higaonna Kanryō, who learned it during his studies in Fuzhou, China, and passed it to his students including Chōjun Miyagi and Kyoda Juhatsu. Miyagi later modified the kata into the closed-fist version used today. In some schools there are two versions: Sanchin Dai Ichi (Miyagi's closed-fist version, sometimes called Sanchin Sho) and Sanchin Dai Ni (Higaonna's older open-hand version). Other schools distinguish between 'Miyagi Sanchin' and 'Higaonna Sanchin' without using Dai Ichi/Dai Ni terminology. Note that the Uechi-ryū version of this kata has a different lineage.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Tensho was created by Chōjun Miyagi around 1921 as a softer counterpart to the hard, linear Sanchin kata. It was inspired by Chinese forms observed during his 1915 trip to Fujian, particularly a form known as Rokkishu (六機手 — Six Hands), which emphasised circular hand movements and breathing. Another school of thought is that Miyagi may have based Tensho on a kata called Kakuha from Higaonna's syllabus. Tensho embodies the 'ju' (soft) aspect of Gōjū-ryū and stands as a complement to Sanchin's hard, muscular quality.
lineage: Rokkishu (Chinese Form) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Seipai is one of the classical Gōjū-ryū kata transmitted through Higaonna Kanryō from Chinese martial arts in Fujian Province. The number 18 refers to 18 fundamental fighting methods contained within the kata, and also holds Buddhist numerological significance, representing the 18 disciples of Buddha or various aspects of enlightenment. The kata is characterised by dynamic shifts between long-range and close-range techniques, emphasising powerful strikes, quick changes in direction, and effective use of angles. Also romanised as Sepai.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi, Kyoda Juhatsu; Chōjun Miyagi → Masutatsu (via Goen Yamaguchi)

history: Kakufa is believed to have been taught or created by Go Kenki (Wu Xianhui), a Chinese tea merchant and martial artist who lived in Okinawa, and is preserved in the lineage of Higa Seiko. It preserves White Crane techniques from the Fujian tradition. Also known as Hakutsuru.
lineage: Go Kenki (Fujian White Crane)

history: Hookiyu is a basic kata or set of techniques created by Seikichi Toguchi of Shorei-Kan Gōjū-ryū. It is sometimes considered a simplified form of the Gekisai kata, and is used in Shorei-Kan Gōjū-ryū as introductory training material.
lineage: Seikichi Toguchi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Gekiha was created by Seikichi Toguchi of Shorei-Kan Gōjū-ryū. It expands on the basics introduced in Hookiyu and is part of the Toguchi introductory curriculum.
lineage: Seikichi Toguchi (Gōjū-ryū)

history: Nipaipo is characterised by its intricate and flowing hand techniques, evasive footwork, and techniques that emphasise joint manipulation, trapping, and rapid-fire strikes, derived from White Crane boxing. It was transmitted to Kenwa Mabuni through the Chinese martial artist Go Kenki (Wu Xianhui), who lived in Okinawa. A version of this kata was adopted into Shōtōkan as Nijuhachiho.
lineage: Chinese White Crane → Go Kenki → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Aoyagi was created by Kenwa Mabuni, the founder of Shitō-ryū, in the 1930s. It is possible that he had input from Yasuhiro Konishi (founder of Shindō Jinen-ryū) and assistance from Ueshiba Morihei, the creator of Aikido. The kata was intended for practical self-defence, especially for women, and may have been specifically created for female railway workers training with Mabuni. The kata is also known as Seiryū in some lineages.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Shinsei was created by Kenwa Mabuni in the early to mid-20th century within the Shitō-ryū school. It translates as 'True Life' or 'New Life', suggesting themes of rebirth and renewal. It is almost identical to Chōjun Miyagi's Gekisai Dai Ni.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Shinpa was composed by Kenwa Mabuni in the early to mid-20th century. Similar to some Kyokushin kata, it was originally incomplete and said to be inspired by Uechi-ryū. It was completed by Mabuni's son, Mabuni Kenei. The name suggests the dynamic interplay of intention and physical execution.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni → Mabuni Kenei (Shitō-ryū)

history: Juroku (also written Jyuroku) translates to 'Sixteen'. It was developed by Kenwa Mabuni in 1941, possibly named after the 16th year of the Showa era. It was designed to teach fundamental techniques and principles, and carries symbolic meaning related to specific principles in Asian martial arts.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Myojo was created by Kenwa Mabuni and named after a Japanese high school where he taught self-defence. It was designed to be accessible and practical, especially for young students and women. It includes simple, effective techniques suitable for beginners.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Matsukaze was created by Kenwa Mabuni. It may be named after a Japanese Noh play of the same name.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Kenshū was composed by Kenwa Mabuni as part of the Shitō-ryū curriculum.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Kensho was composed by Kenwa Mabuni as part of the Shitō-ryū curriculum.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Kenpaku was composed by Kenwa Mabuni as part of the Shitō-ryū curriculum.
lineage: Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Happo Papporen (also called Papuren) was learned by Kenwa Mabuni from the Chinese martial artist Go Kenki, who brought White Crane techniques to Okinawa.
lineage: Go Kenki (White Crane) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Hakutsuru (also written Hakkaku or Haffa) represents Chinese White Crane boxing (Hakkaku ken). Kenwa Mabuni learned this form from Go Kenki, a Chinese martial artist and tea merchant living in Okinawa.
lineage: White Crane → Go Kenki → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

translation: Southern Peace / Peace from the South
history: Annanko (also written Anan) is a kata practised in the Ryūei-ryū system and adopted into Shitō-ryū. The name likely refers to Annam, the historical name for Vietnam, suggesting Chinese or Vietnamese origins.
lineage: Ryūei-ryū → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Niseishi is the Shitō-ryū version of the kata known as Nijushiho in Shōtōkan. It retains closer ties to the original Aragaki form. A variant called Aragaki Niseishi is also practised. The kata likely descended from Southern Chinese martial arts.
lineage: Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Rōhai Shodan is one of three versions of the Rōhai kata preserved in Shitō-ryū from which Shōtōkan's Meikyo is derived. The three versions (Shodan, Nidan, Sandan) were taught by Itosu Ankō and preserved by Kenwa Mabuni.
lineage: Kōsaku Matsumora (Tomari-te) → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Rōhai Nidan is the second of three versions of the Rōhai kata preserved in Shitō-ryū. They were taught by Itosu Ankō and preserved by Kenwa Mabuni. Shōtōkan's Meikyo is derived from the three Rōhai versions.
lineage: Kōsaku Matsumora (Tomari-te) → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Rōhai Sandan is the third of three versions of the Rōhai kata preserved in Shitō-ryū. They were taught by Itosu Ankō and preserved by Kenwa Mabuni. Shōtōkan's Meikyo is derived from the three Rōhai versions.
lineage: Kōsaku Matsumora (Tomari-te) → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: Sushiho is Kyokushin's version of Gojūshiho/Useishi, emphasising direct, powerful techniques characteristic of Kyokushin's approach. It was adapted from the Shōtōkan version by Masutatsu Ōyama.
lineage: Shuri-te → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: Yantsu is believed to have Southern Chinese origins, likely from the White Crane tradition (unconfirmed). It was introduced to Okinawa in the early 20th century and is associated with the Naha-te tradition. The kata found its way into Kyokushin through Masutatsu Ōyama's training connections to Gōjū-ryū masters, particularly through the lineage of Chōjun Miyagi's students. A version of this kata exists in Shitō-ryū called Ansan/Hansan, and it is possible that Ōyama's Yantsu is a derivation of that kata.
lineage: Chinese White Crane → Okinawan Karate → Shitō-ryū → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: Tsuki no Kata translates as 'Punching Kata' and metaphorically as 'Kata of Fortune'. Note that one form of writing 'tsuki' is 月 meaning 'moon', so the kata is sometimes referred to as 'Form of the Moon'. The lineage flows from Chinese White Crane through Tada Seigo to Gōjū-ryū, then to Kyokushin via Tadashi Nakamura, one of Masutatsu Ōyama's senior students who had extensive Gōjū-ryū background. Ōyama further developed it as a crucial training tool for his full-contact style.
lineage: Chinese Martial Arts → Gōjū-ryū Karate → Tadashi Nakamura or Seigo Tada → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: Garyū was created by Masutatsu Ōyama himself, developed specifically for Kyokushin Karate in the mid-20th century. He named the kata after his pen name (Garyū — Reclining Dragon). The name evokes a sense of latent power and wisdom, like a dragon at rest. Ōyama used this kata to emphasise the martial philosophy and technical prowess within the Kyokushin curriculum.
lineage: Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: Sokugi Taikyoku is modelled along the lines of the Funakoshi Taikyoku kata but with the emphasis on kicking techniques (sokugi is equivalent to ashi waza — foot techniques). It was created after Masutatsu Ōyama's death by Shōgō Kuniba (1935–1992).
lineage: Shōgō Kuniba (Kyokushin lineage)

history: Anan likely refers to the region of Vietnam historically called Annam. The kata emphasises practical self-defence applications with close-quarters fighting techniques and joint manipulations. It likely dates to the 19th century, originating from the village fighting traditions of northern Okinawa. Norisato Nakaima is credited with bringing the kata to Naha after learning it during his study in China. Anan Dai is a more advanced version of the Anan kata (often called Anan Sho).
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: Paiho (also written Paipho, Paihoh, or Pai Fa) originated from Southern Chinese quanfa, specifically White Crane boxing. It was brought to Okinawa by Norisato Nakaima during his training in Fuzhou in the mid-19th century and preserved in the Ryūei-ryū system.
lineage: Chinese White Crane → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: Ohan Sho is one of two versions of Ohan (Sho and Dai) that are unique to Ryūei-ryū. They were transmitted through Norisato Nakaima from Chinese or Vietnamese sources.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: Ohan Dai is one of two versions of Ohan (Sho and Dai) that are unique to Ryūei-ryū. They were transmitted through Norisato Nakaima from Chinese or Vietnamese sources.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

translation: Peace from the South / Peaceful Southern Sky
history: Ananku translates to 'Peace from the South' or 'Peaceful Southern Sky', with 'Annan' historically referring to Vietnam (Annam), suggesting possible Southeast Asian martial arts influences. The kata has uncertain origins but likely developed in Okinawa during the 18th or early 19th century. One theory is that Chōtoku Kyan brought this form back to the Tomari region from Taiwan in 1895, though it is more likely that Kyan created it with strong Chinese quanfa influences. It is probably the most well-known kata unique to Shōrin-ryū.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Chōtoku Kyan → Shōrin-ryū

history: Seichin translates as 'Ten Battles', though it is typically described as 'Controlled Battle'. The number ten symbolises a significant stage of maturity in Okinawan culture. This is one of the kata created by Kanbun Uechi after returning from China. The current Uechi-ryū version was standardised by Saburo Uehara in the 1950s, although alternative sources state it was created by Seiki Itokazu. In most Uechi-ryū circles, 'Saburō no kata' is used as an alternative name for Seichin.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Kanbun Uechi → Saburo Uehara / Seiki Itokazu (Uechi-ryū)

history: Seiryū translates as '16' but is sometimes called 'Blue Dragon' or 'Azure Dragon', representing one of the four celestial guardians in East Asian mythology. The current Uechi-ryū version was created by Kanei Uechi in the 1950s.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Kanbun Uechi → Kanei Uechi (Uechi-ryū)

history: Kanchin translates to 'Kanbun's Battle' or 'Complete Battle', honouring Kanbun Uechi, the founder of Uechi-ryū. It was created by Kanei Uechi, the son of Kanbun Uechi, in the 1950s. It was potentially developed as a bridge between the classical Sanchin and the more advanced Seisan kata.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Kanbun Uechi → Kanei Uechi → Saburo Uehara (Uechi-ryū)

history: Kanshiwa is named after Kanbun Uechi and Shu Shiwa, his Chinese teacher. Along with Kanshu, it was created by Kanei Uechi as a beginner kata sometime after his father's death. It serves as an introductory kata to bridge the gap between Sanchin and the more advanced classical forms, and is typically the first non-Sanchin kata taught in Uechi-ryū.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Kanbun Uechi → Kanei Uechi (Uechi-ryū)

history: Kanshu was created by Kanei Uechi as part of the expanded Uechi-ryū curriculum to complement Kanshiwa and provide additional training pathways within the system.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Kanbun Uechi → Kanei Uechi (Uechi-ryū)

history: Sunsu is unique to Isshin-ryū and was created by Tatsuo Shimabuku, the founder of Isshin-ryū. The name is a rendering of Shimabuku's nickname. It is considered the signature and most advanced kata of the style, incorporating techniques drawn from Shimabuku's various teachers.
lineage: Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Heian Shodan (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's Heian. The kata shares the same base as Shōtōkan Heian Shodan but is executed with Wadō-ryū's characteristic emphasis on natural body movement, evasion (tai sabaki), and fluid transitions rather than the more linear Shōtōkan approach.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Heian Nidan (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's Heian. The kata shares the same base as Shōtōkan Heian Nidan but is executed with Wadō-ryū's characteristic emphasis on natural body movement, evasion (tai sabaki), and fluid transitions.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Heian Sandan (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's Heian. The kata shares the same base as Shōtōkan Heian Sandan but is executed with Wadō-ryū's characteristic emphasis on natural body movement and evasion.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Heian Yondan (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's Heian. The kata shares the same base as Shōtōkan Heian Yondan but is executed with Wadō-ryū's characteristic emphasis on natural body movement and evasion.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Heian Godan (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's Heian. The kata shares the same base as Shōtōkan Heian Godan but is executed with Wadō-ryū's characteristic emphasis on natural body movement and evasion.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Kankū Dai (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū's version retains the original Okinawan name Kushanku rather than Funakoshi's Kankū Dai. It is the same base kata, executed with Wadō-ryū's emphasis on flowing body movement and evasion.
lineage: Kūsankū (Chinese Diplomat) → Kanga Sakugawa → Itosu Ankō → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Tekki Shodan (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū's version retains the original Okinawan name Naihanchi rather than Funakoshi's Tekki Shodan. It is the same base kata.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Hangetsu (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū's version retains the original Okinawan name Seishan rather than Funakoshi's Hangetsu. It is the same base kata but the execution differs — Wadō-ryū maintains more of the original fluid quality rather than the deep stances and pronounced breathing of Shōtōkan.
lineage: Naha-te (Seisan) → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Wadō-ryū variant of Gankaku (Shōtōkan). Wadō-ryū's version retains the original Okinawan name Chintō rather than Funakoshi's Gankaku. It is the same base kata, performed with Wadō-ryū's characteristic body evasion and fluidity.
lineage: Chintō (Chinese Sailor) → Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Hironori Ōtsuka (Wadō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Heian Shodan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan. This is the Shitō-ryū version of Shōtōkan's Heian Shodan, sharing the same Itosu Ankō lineage but executed in Shitō-ryū style.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Heian Nidan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan. This is the Shitō-ryū version of Shōtōkan's Heian Nidan.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Heian Sandan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan. This is the Shitō-ryū version of Shōtōkan's Heian Sandan.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Heian Yondan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Pinan. This is the Shitō-ryū version of Shōtōkan's Heian Yondan.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Tekki Shodan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Naifanchi. This is essentially the same kata as Shōtōkan's Tekki Shodan, the original complete Naihanchi form.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Tekki Nidan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Naifanchi. This is essentially the same kata as Shōtōkan's Tekki Nidan.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Tekki Sandan (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original Okinawan name Naifanchi. This is essentially the same kata as Shōtōkan's Tekki Sandan.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Bassai Dai (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Bassai Dai shares the same Passai base as Shōtōkan's Bassai Dai. A specific regional version, Tomari Bassai, is also preserved in some Shitō-ryū schools.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Bassai Sho (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Bassai Sho shares the same Passai base as Shōtōkan's Bassai Sho.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Kankū Dai (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original name Kūsankū rather than Funakoshi's Kankū. It shares the same base kata as Shōtōkan's Kankū Dai. A version called Shiho Kusanku also exists in some Shitō-ryū schools.
lineage: Kūsankū (Chinese Diplomat) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Kankū Sho (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original name Kūsankū rather than Funakoshi's Kankū. It shares the same base kata as Shōtōkan's Kankū Sho.
lineage: Kūsankū (Chinese Diplomat) → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Empi (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original name Wanshū rather than Funakoshi's Empi. It is the same base kata.
lineage: Wang Ji → Tomari-te Masters → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Gankaku (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the original name Chintō rather than Funakoshi's Gankaku. It is the same base kata.
lineage: Chintō (Chinese Sailor) → Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Jion (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Jion shares the same base as Shōtōkan's Jion, from the Tomari-te Temple Kata group.
lineage: Tomari-te School → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Jitte (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Jitte shares the same base as Shōtōkan's Jitte, from the Tomari-te Temple Kata group.
lineage: Tomari-te School → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Jiin (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Jiin shares the same base as Shōtōkan's Jiin, from the Tomari-te Temple Kata group.
lineage: Tomari-te School → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Sanchin (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Sanchin shares the same Gōjū-ryū lineage and structure. Mabuni studied under both Itosu Ankō and Higaonna Kanryō, bringing this kata into Shitō-ryū.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Tensho (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Tensho shares the same lineage as Gōjū-ryū Tensho.
lineage: Rokkishu (Chinese Form) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Saifa (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Saifa shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage. Mabuni's study under Higaonna Kanryō brought this kata into Shitō-ryū.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Seienchin (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Seiunchin shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Sanseiru (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Sanseru shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Shisōchin (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Shisōchin shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Seipai (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Sepai shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage. Also romanised as Seipai.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Kururunfa (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Kururunfa shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Suparinpei (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Suparinpei shares the same Naha-te / Gōjū-ryū lineage.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Sōchin (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Sōchin is a sister kata to Shōtōkan Sōchin. Mabuni is said to have remained closer to the original Aragaki form of this kata than the Shōtōkan version.
lineage: Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Unsu (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū retains the name Unshu. It is the same base kata as Shōtōkan's Unsu.
lineage: Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Seisan (Gōjū-ryū). Shitō-ryū Seisan shares the same base kata as Gōjū-ryū Seisan and Shōtōkan's Hangetsu, though stylistically very different across styles. Lineage comes through both Higaonna Kanryō and Aragaki Seishō.
lineage: Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) / Aragaki Seishō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Shitō-ryū variant of Gojūshiho Dai (Shōtōkan). Shitō-ryū Gojūshiho shares the same Useishi base as Shōtōkan's Gojūshiho. Mabuni preserved multiple versions.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Itosu Ankō → Kenwa Mabuni (Shitō-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Heian Shodan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin retains the original name Pinan and adds 'Sono Ichi' (Number One). It is based on the same Shōtōkan Heian Shodan but performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power, deeper stances, and audible ibuki breathing.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Heian Nidan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin's version of Heian Nidan, performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power and deeper stances.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Heian Sandan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin's version of Heian Sandan, performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power and deeper stances.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Heian Yondan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin's version of Heian Yondan, performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power and deeper stances.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Heian Godan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin's version of Heian Godan, performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power and deeper stances.
lineage: Kushanku/Channan → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) [Pinan] → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Kankū Dai (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin Kankū Dai is similar to Shōtōkan's Kankū Dai but performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power and ibuki breathing emphasis.
lineage: Kūsankū → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Tekki Shodan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin Naihanchi is similar to Shōtōkan's Tekki Shodan, retaining the original Okinawan name.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Gekisai Dai Ichi (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted the Gōjū-ryū Gekisai kata. Performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power emphasis and ibuki breathing.
lineage: Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Gekisai Dai Ni (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted the Gōjū-ryū Gekisai kata. Performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power emphasis and ibuki breathing.
lineage: Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Tensho (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted Gōjū-ryū Tensho. It is performed with pronounced ibuki breathing reflecting Kyokushin's emphasis on breath control.
lineage: Rokkishu (Chinese Form) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Sanchin (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted Gōjū-ryū Sanchin. It is a cornerstone of Kyokushin training, emphasising internal tension, controlled breathing, and mental focus.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Saifa (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted Gōjū-ryū Saifa, known in Kyokushin as Saiha. Performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Seienchin (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted Gōjū-ryū Seienchin. Performed with Kyokushin's characteristic power and stance depth.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Seipai (Gōjū-ryū). Kyokushin adopted Gōjū-ryū Seipai.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Higaonna Kanryō (Naha-te) → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Bassai Dai (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin Bassai is similar to Shōtōkan's Bassai Dai. Oyama removed it from the official curriculum but it was reinstated by some schools after his death.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Taikyoku Shodan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin Taikyoku Sono Ichi is similar to Shōtōkan's Taikyoku Shodan. In Kyokushin it is also practised in 'ura' (reverse) form.
lineage: Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Taikyoku Shodan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin Taikyoku Sono Ni is based on the Shōtōkan Taikyoku series. In Kyokushin it is also practised in 'ura' (reverse) form.
lineage: Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Kyokushin variant of Taikyoku Shodan (Shōtōkan). Kyokushin Taikyoku Sono San is based on the Shōtōkan Taikyoku series. In Kyokushin it is also practised in 'ura' (reverse) form.
lineage: Gichin Funakoshi (Shōtōkan) → Masutatsu Ōyama (Kyokushin)

history: NOTE: This is a Ryūei-ryū variant of Sanchin (Gōjū-ryū). The Ryūei-ryū version of Sanchin is virtually the same as that in Gōjū-ryū but potentially via a different lineage, thought to have been transmitted directly through Ryu Ryu Ko rather than via Higaonna Kanryō.
lineage: Ryu Ryu Ko (Chinese) → Norisato Nakaima (Ryūei-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Ryūei-ryū variant of Seisan (Gōjū-ryū). Ryūei-ryū Sēsan is similar to versions in Gōjū-ryū and Uechi-ryū. It was transmitted through Norisato Nakaima from Chinese sources.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: NOTE: This is a Ryūei-ryū variant of Pachū/Paiku (Shitō-ryū). Ryūei-ryū Pāchū is similar to versions in Shitō-ryū. It was transmitted through Norisato Nakaima from Chinese sources.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: NOTE: This is a Ryūei-ryū variant of Heiku (Shitō-ryū). Ryūei-ryū Heikū is similar to versions in Shitō-ryū. It was transmitted through Norisato Nakaima from Chinese sources.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: NOTE: This is a Ryūei-ryū variant of Seienchin (Gōjū-ryū). Ryūei-ryū Seyonchin is similar to the Seiunchin kata in Gōjū-ryū and Shitō-ryū. Transmitted through Norisato Nakaima.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: NOTE: This is a Ryūei-ryū variant of Paiku (Shitō-ryū). Ryūei-ryū Paikū is similar to versions in Shitō-ryū. Transmitted through Norisato Nakaima from Chinese sources.
lineage: Possibly Vietnamese/Chinese → Norisato Nakaima → Ryūei-ryū

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Seisan (Gōjū-ryū). Isshin-ryū Seisan resembles the Shuri-te version passed on by Chōtoku Kyan and shares features with Gōjū-ryū Seisan.
lineage: Shuri-te (Kyan lineage) → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Seienchin (Gōjū-ryū). Isshin-ryū Seiunchin is similar to Gōjū-ryū Seiunchin.
lineage: Gōjū-ryū lineage → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Tekki Shodan (Shōtōkan). Isshin-ryū Naihanchi is similar to Shōtōkan Tekki Shodan. The Isshin-ryū version starts left rather than right. Some schools also practise a version that combines elements of all three Naihanchi.
lineage: Sōkon Matsumura → Itosu Ankō (Shuri-te) → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Empi (Shōtōkan). Isshin-ryū Wanshū is similar to Shōtōkan Empi, retaining the original Okinawan name.
lineage: Wang Ji → Tomari-te masters → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Sanchin (Gōjū-ryū). Isshin-ryū favours the shorter Miyagi version of Sanchin.
lineage: Chinese martial arts → Chōjun Miyagi (Gōjū-ryū) → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Gankaku (Shōtōkan). Isshin-ryū Chintō is similar to Shōtōkan Gankaku, retaining the original Okinawan name.
lineage: Chintō (Chinese Sailor) → Sōkon Matsumura (Shuri-te) → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Isshin-ryū variant of Kankū Dai (Shōtōkan). Isshin-ryū Kūsankū is a version of the root Kūsankū kata shared by Shōtōkan Kankū Dai, retaining the original Okinawan name.
lineage: Kūsankū (Chinese Diplomat) → Kanga Sakugawa → Tatsuo Shimabuku (Isshin-ryū)

history: NOTE: This is a Matsubayashi-ryū variant of Tekki Shodan (Shōtōkan). Matsubayashi-ryū Naihanchi shares the same Shuri-te roots as Shōtōkan's Tekki Shodan, retaining the original Okinawan name.
lineage: Shuri-te/Tomari-te → Shōrin-ryū → Matsubayashi-ryū

history: NOTE: This is a Matsubayashi-ryū variant of Bassai Dai (Shōtōkan). Matsubayashi-ryū Passai retains the original Okinawan name. It shares the same Shuri-te roots as Shōtōkan's Bassai Dai.
lineage: Shuri-te/Tomari-te → Shōrin-ryū → Matsubayashi-ryū
